html:
The Battle of Passchendaele, or Third Battle of Ypres, was a British offensive in Flanders from July to November 1917. It became a byword for the futility of the First World War.

The British commander Douglas Haig aimed to break out of the Ypres salient and reach the Belgian coast. Heavy shelling destroyed the drainage of the low fields, and the wettest August in years turned them into a sea of mud where men and horses drowned. Canadian troops finally took the ruined village of Passchendaele in November, a gain of about eight kilometres.

Each side lost around a quarter of a million men or more. Ypres had already seen the first large use of poison gas in 1915. The cemeteries and memorials around it, such as the Menin Gate, still draw many visitors. See Belgium, the occupation, and the Somme.
